scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In February 1600, English actor William Kempe danced more than a hundred miles from London to Norwich, turning a humble jig into legendary endurance theater.
This is Jig. 16th century.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (ZYa52bTmpB8)
Title card: Jig · Ireland · 16th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The term jig derives from the French giguer, meaning to jump, or the Italian giga, with roots in the Old English giga.

In 16th-century England, jigs served as popular post-play theatrical entertainments featuring dance and pantomime, exemplified by William Kempe's legendary 1600 endurance dance from London to Norwich.
During the 16th and 17th centuries, the dance was adopted in Ireland and Scotland, later crossing to mainland Europe where it became the concluding movement of the Baroque suite.
on_screen: Map: Ireland · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Jigs are performed during festive community gatherings, competitive feiseanna, theatrical performances, and seasonal rituals.

Historically associated with communal celebration and dramatic farce, the dance serves as a vital marker of cultural identity and physical endurance across Irish, Scottish, English, and diaspora communities.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The jig is danced primarily in compound meters such as 6/8, 9/8, and 12/8 time.

In Irish step dance, light jigs feature rapid footwork where feet stay close to the ground using the rising step, while slip jigs in 9/8 time utilize graceful, high-toe movements that glide across the floor.
Treble jigs introduce hard shoes with loud stomps, trebles, and clicks.
Watch for rising step.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Jig music is characterized by compound time signatures, overwhelmingly structured around two eight-bar parts (AABB).
Traditional melodies rely heavily on eighth notes and quarter-eighth note pairs.
Listen for the fiddle, pipe and tabor, five-string banjo, melodeon.
The pulse is 6/8 at about 116 beats a minute.
Rapid bouncing compound meter tunes driven by fiddles and accordions, pulsing with alternating strong and weak beats.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes vary widely by tradition, ranging from modern competitive Irish solo dresses and soft ghillies or hard shoes to traditional Morris dance whites adorned with ribbons and bells.
Settings span Elizabethan public theaters, 19th-century minstrel stages, competitive feiseanna halls, and village squares during regional Italian and Occitan festivals.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical figures include William Kempe, the Elizabethan actor and dancer famous for his London-to-Norwich journey; Master Juba (William Henry Lane), the 19th-century African-American minstrel dancer who revolutionized step dancing; John Diamond, his prominent white competitor; and 19th-century sand dancers Kitty O'Neil and Howard 'Sandman' Sims.

Regional expressions include the Irish light, slip, single, and treble jigs; the English Morris jig and bacca-pipes; the Scottish country jig; the French Canadian traditional jig; the Métis jig; and Italian variants such as the Emilian giga, the Quattro province giga, and the ritual Lachera of Rocca Grimalda.

The jig descends from 16th-century British folk dance and theatrical farces, branching into Baroque concert suites (gigue/giga), Irish and Scottish traditional step and country dances, 19th-century minstrel and sand dances, and modern competitive step forms.
